# Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 24 (Bi-Vb Pc24)

**ID:** Bi-Vb Pc24
**Section:** Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga (bi-vb)
**Collection:** Vinaya
**Title (Pali):** Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 24
**Title (English, from literature):** Moving robes
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/vin02m1.mul7.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 24 (also known as the *Saṅghāṭicāra-sikkhāpada*) is a disciplinary rule in the Vinaya Piṭaka regulating a nun's care of her robes. According to the rule, a nun who leaves any of her five robes untouched for five consecutive days commits an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) that must be confessed [Bechert et al. 1997]. While the origin story itself does not mention the five-day time limit—introducing it only in the formal precept—the canonical word analysis (*padabhājaniya*) clarifies the phrase *pañcāhikaṁ saṅghāṭicāraṁ atikkāmeti* to mean that if on the fifth day a nun neither wears, puts on, nor airs any of her five monastic robes in the sun, she transgresses the rule [Bechert et al. 1997; Hüsken 1997].

Scholars note that although the compound refers to the outer cloak (*saṅghāṭi*), the canonical commentary broadens the scope to encompass the entire requisite five-robe set of a nun [Bechert et al. 1997]. In the textual transmission, the Thai edition presents the variant reading *saṅghāṭivāra* ("the time-period for the outer robe") both in the Vinaya text and its commentary, the *Samantapāsādikā* [Hüsken 1997]. Commentarial discussions in the *Samantapāsādikā* address practical dilemmas under this rule, such as non-offense scenarios where a nun is prevented from handling or exposing a valuable robe due to fear of thieves [Hüsken 1997]. Modern translations include an English rendering by Bhikkhu Brahmali.

Curated parallels include the Theravāda *Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha* (Pc 24) and *Bhikkhunī Parivāra* (Pc 24), alongside Chinese Vinaya parallels in the Dharmaguptaka (*Lzh Dg Bi Vb Pc 104* and its Pātimokkha) and Sarvāstivāda traditions (*Lzh Sarv Bi Vb Pc 131* and its Pātimokkha).
